qs.q: A patient with newly diagnosed Addison's disease due to an autoimmune etiology is expected to show which histological feature upon biopsy of the adrenal glands?
o: Bilateral hemorrhagic necrosis involving the medulla
Small atrophic glands with lymphocytic infiltration
A large, irregular, necrotic mass with pleomorphic cells
qs.e: Autoimmune adrenal insufficiency is characterized morphologically by small atrophic glands with lymphocytic infiltration and cortical fibrosis. Caseating granulomas are typical of tuberculous adrenalitis.

qs.q: A patient with long-term rheumatoid arthritis managed with high-dose oral corticosteroids develops central obesity, a moon face, and purple striae. What is the most likely morphological change in the patient's adrenal glands?
qs.e: Exogenous steroid use is the most common overall cause of Cushing's syndrome and leads to bilateral adrenal atrophy due to suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis. Endogenous ACTH-dependent causes like pituitary adenomas lead to bilateral adrenal hyperplasia.

qs.q: A 48-year-old woman undergoes resection of a 120g adrenal gland mass. Gross examination shows a grey-white, irregular tumor with necrosis, and histology confirms vascular invasion. What single diagnostic feature is considered definitive for malignancy in this lesion?
qs.e: Vascular or capsular invasion, alongside metastasis, is required to definitively diagnose an adrenal carcinoma as cytology alone is insufficient. Uniform clear cells and a suppressed ACTH level are typical features of benign adenomas rather than markers of malignancy.

qs.q: Which hormone is secreted by the adrenal glands, with abnormal circulating levels pointing toward primary adrenal dysfunction?
qs.e: Cortisol is secreted by the adrenal glands and abnormal levels indicate adrenal dysfunction. Thyroxine is secreted by the thyroid gland.

qs.q: A patient presents with a lung tumour that has metastasized to the adrenal glands. Why is adrenal insufficiency uncommon despite near-total obliteration of the glands?
qs.e: Adrenal insufficiency is uncommon in lung cancer metastases because islands of functional cortical cells persist even when the glands are nearly obliterated. The metastases are malignant, and the tumour does not typically secrete cortisol to compensate.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is true regarding the adrenal glands? ---
o: 17α-hydroxylase is found in the zona fasciculata
Zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone; zona reticularis makes androgens. ACTH feedback is from cortisol, not androgens.
The zona glomerulosa primarily produces glucocorticoids
There is negative feedback from androgens on ACTH
The zona fasciculata produces active androgens
qs.e: The zona fasciculata contains steroidogenic enzymes including 17α-hydroxylase and primarily produces glucocorticoids such as cortisol.

qs.q: A patient with lung cancer has adrenal glands nearly obliterated by metastases on CT but shows no clinical signs of adrenal insufficiency. This is explained by
o: The opposite adrenal gland enlarges to compensate, providing adequate cortisol levels.
The lung tumor secretes cortisol ectopically, concealing signs of adrenal failure.
Small remaining cortical cell islands produce enough hormone to sustain normal adrenal activity.
Metastases destroy medullary tissue first while completely preserving cortical function.
qs.e: Even when adrenal glands are nearly obliterated by metastatic tumour, residual islands of cortical cells persist and produce sufficient cortisol to prevent clinical Addison disease.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The adrenal glands sit atop the kidneys, each with an outer cortex and inner medulla. Their structure determines hormone output and clinical signs when damaged or diseased.

sections.p: Adrenal glands are paired, triangular organs on the kidney hilum. They produce steroids and catecholamines that regulate stress, blood pressure, and metabolism.
Each gland has an outer cortex (zona glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis) and an inner medulla. The cortex is divided into three zones by hormone type.
Adrenals sit posterior to the liver (right) and spleen (left), anterior to the diaphragm, and adjacent to the renal vessels.
Rich arterial supply from the superior, middle, and inferior adrenal arteries; venous drainage via a central vein into the renal vein (right) or IVC (left).

t.b: Shows arterial supply and detects aneurysms; abnormal flow suggests pheochromocytoma

sections.p: Sympathetic fibers innervate the medulla; parasympathetic input is minimal.
Cortex secretes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), glucocorticoids (cortisol), and adrenal androgens. Medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine.
Damage or tumors alter hormone output, causing hypertension, hypoglycemia, or adrenal crisis. Pheochromocytoma presents with episodic hypertension and headaches.

t.b: Low cortisol with high ACTH suggests primary adrenal insufficiency
Elevated in pheochromocytoma; normal in other causes of hypertension

sections.p: Remember the adrenal gland’s dual function: steroid hormones from cortex, catecholamines from medulla. In surgery, removal of the left gland can precipitate hypotension due to loss of aldosterone.
